html:
The flight of most of the Hindu Pandits of the Kashmir valley in Indian-administered Kashmir, mainly in early 1990, as an armed Muslim separatist insurgency took hold.

The Pandits, Kashmiri-speaking Brahmins, had lived in the valley for many centuries as a small minority; Lal Ded and many Sanskrit scholars of old Kashmir came from their world. In 1989 an insurgency broke out against Indian rule, part of the long Kashmir conflict that began at Partition. Militants killed a number of Pandit officials and public figures, threats were posted and broadcast, and fear spread.

Of a Pandit population of roughly 120,000 to 140,000, some 90,000 to 100,000 left the valley by the middle of 1990, most for Jammu and Delhi, where many lived for years in camps. Why it happened so fast is still argued: some stress the militants' threats, others the role of the state governor's policies. Very few have returned, and the exodus remains a bitter issue in Indian politics.
sum: The flight of most of the Hindu Pandits of the Kashmir valley in Indian-administered Kashmir, mainly in early 1990, as an armed Muslim separatist insurgency took hold.
